How does autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity build a regression whose variance responds to its own recent shocks, and how does that compare to letting an outside variable drive volatility instead?

Autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity writes the conditional variance of a regression disturbance as a function of its own recent squared values rather than of an external driver, giving a compact alternative to exogenous-variable or bilinear volatility specifications.

Why go to the trouble of modeling heteroscedasticity directly rather than patching forecast errors with a rough variance proxy, when the same size-clustering could just as easily signal a missing regressor or an unnoticed break?

Heteroscedasticity in forecast errors motivates explicit variance modeling because portfolio theory ties the price of risk to time-varying variance, and ruling out an omitted regressor or a structural shift as the real cause secures such a model against misspecification.

How is maximum likelihood estimation set up for a regression with time-varying conditional variance, and does assuming normal errors simplify the resulting information matrix when the variance function is linear?

Maximum likelihood estimation of a regression with time-varying conditional variance builds its log likelihood and score from the assumed normal density, and a linear variance specification lets the information matrix take a simplified closed form.

What moment existence conditions must a first-order ARCH process satisfy for its variance and higher moments to stay finite, and why do the odd moments vanish?

Moment existence conditions for a first-order ARCH process require its autoregressive parameter to stay within a bounded range, and within that range the symmetry of the innovation distribution forces every odd moment to vanish.

Covariance stationarity conditions for a higher-order conditionally heteroscedastic process reduce to a root restriction on its characteristic equation, a restriction that can also be checked against exponential or absolute-value variance forms.

Before trusting an estimation theory built on a conditionally heteroscedastic model, what regularity conditions -- covering the shape and boundedness of the variance function -- need to hold, and does a simple linear form clear that bar?

A workable set of regularity conditions demands that the variance function stay symmetric and within finite bounds, properties that secure the key expectations any later estimation argument leans on; a simple linear form clears this bar without much trouble.

Does block diagonality of the information matrix let a practitioner fit the mean and volatility parts of a conditionally heteroscedastic regression as two separate, equally efficient problems, and what property of the underlying disturbance makes that split legitimate?

Block diagonality of the information matrix splits a conditionally heteroscedastic regression's fitting problem in two, letting the mean coefficients be pinned down with no efficiency cost from ignoring the volatility side, a split that traces back to a symmetric error distribution.

A scoring algorithm updates the mean and variance parameters of a conditionally heteroscedastic regression step by step toward the likelihood maximum, halting under a gradient-based rule and yielding estimates with a known limiting distribution.

The relative efficiency of maximum likelihood estimation climbs as the data's volatility clustering grows more pronounced, a gain worth chasing even though the simpler least-squares fit never stops being unbiased and consistent on its own.

A Lagrange multiplier test for conditional heteroscedasticity can be computed from routine regression residuals alone, offering a cheap screening step that avoids an iterative variance-estimation procedure when the disturbance pattern is absent.

Outlier diagnostics applied after fitting a conditionally heteroscedastic model can show tighter, better-calibrated confidence intervals than a constant-variance alternative, evidenced by fewer residuals crossing the expected threshold and a different timing among the exceptions that remain.
